q: What is the SDLC and why does it still matter for ML projects?
short: The structured loop of planning, analysis, design, development, testing, deployment and maintenance. ML systems are still software: they need requirements, design, tests, deployment and maintenance, with extra loops for data and models.
detail: ML adds data collection, training, evaluation and monitoring stages but doesn't replace the SDLC.
example: A churn model needs an API, CI/CD and on-call support like any service.
mistakes: Treating ML as a one-off research project.

q: Data engineer vs data scientist vs ML engineer?
short: Data engineers build pipelines and storage; data scientists explore data and build models and insights; ML engineers deploy, monitor and retrain models in production and close the feedback loop.
example: ETL to warehouse; demand forecast; churn API with monitoring.
follow: Which is most critical early on?
mistakes: Assuming one person can skip the lower levels.

q: Explain the data science hierarchy of needs.
short: Collect → move/store → explore/transform → aggregate/label → learn/optimise → AI/deep learning. Each level depends on the ones below; most effort and failures live in the lower levels.
example: A team without logging cannot train a recommender.

q: Why is ML harder to engineer than ordinary software?
short: Three axes change (code, data, model) instead of one; behaviour is probabilistic and learned, so it can't be fully specified; models degrade as the world changes and must be monitored and retrained.
detail: Continuous delivery for ML must version all three.
example: Same code, new data → different model.

q: Describe the model workflow.
short: Development (train, tune, evaluate) → versioning → deployment → monitoring (drift, degradation, bias) → retraining, as a loop.
detail: Each retrained model is a new version.

q: Training vs inference?
short: Training learns model parameters from historical data; inference applies the fixed trained model to new data to produce predictions.
detail: Different compute profiles and failure modes.
example: Nightly training job vs real-time API.

q: What are the three generations of ML?
short: 1: classical ML on labelled data; 2: deep learning on big data; 3: transfer learning/Transformers, often consumed via APIs with little or no training.
example: Calling an LLM API for summarisation.
follow: What new risks does generation 3 bring?

q: What is a foundation model?
short: A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks with minimal task-specific tuning (fine-tuning, prompting, transfer learning); LLMs are the best-known example.

q: How do SE and ML differ in specification and evaluation?
short: SE functions have precise contracts and are judged by functional correctness; ML functions are specified by examples and judged by statistical accuracy because exact rules can't be written.
follow: How do you write ML requirements?

q: What does cloud-native mean?
short: Building and running scalable applications in dynamic environments using agile + DevOps + microservices + containers + cloud.
example: A containerised model service on Kubernetes.

q: A data scientist hands you a notebook with a 0.92 AUC model. What do you need before production?
short: Reproducible training code and data snapshot, versioned model artifact, input schema and validation, serving API, tests (data, model, infrastructure), latency/cost targets, monitoring and alerting, retraining plan, rollback.
detail: Agree goals and acceptance thresholds with the business.
mistakes: Copying the notebook into an API unchanged.

q: Why must code, data and model be versioned together?
short: A model is a function of all three; changing any one changes behaviour. Reproducing, auditing or rolling back a prediction requires the exact code commit, data snapshot and model artifact/config.
example: Code example ex2: identical inputs → identical run-id.
follow: How do you version large datasets?

q: What changes in the SDLC when moving to AI-assisted development (ADLC)?
short: AI assists with documentation, code, tests and deployment scripts within scaled agile; benefits are speed, consistency and less dependence on individuals; risks are quality and governance of AI-generated artefacts.
example: AI-generated unit tests reviewed in PRs.

q: Your company wants an LLM-based support assistant. Which engineering concerns remain even with no training?
short: Requirements and evaluation sets, prompt and model versioning, RAG data pipelines, latency and token cost, privacy of customer data, safety guardrails, monitoring of quality and hallucinations, fallbacks.
detail: Generation 3 shifts work, it doesn't remove it.

q: Why is the data engineer often the first hire for an ML team?
short: Because the hierarchy of needs starts with collection, movement and storage; without reliable data pipelines, no model can be trained or monitored.
example: Logging checkout events before building a recommender.

q: Model-centric vs system-centric thinking for a new feature?
short: Model-centric tunes algorithms and features for accuracy; system-centric designs data flow, infrastructure, deployment, UX and monitoring for reliable real-world value.
mistakes: Optimising accuracy no one can use.

q: How would you explain the four AI service families to a product manager?
short: Language (understand/generate text), speech (speech↔text, translation, speaker ID), vision (images/video: detection, faces, classification, restoration), decision (recommendations).
detail: Cloud providers package them as APIs.
mistakes: Picking a service before defining the goal.

q: Write a docstring-level spec for a spam classifier.
short: Inputs (email text, metadata), output (probability of spam), acceptance criteria (e.g. precision ≥ 0.98 at recall ≥ 0.9 on a labelled holdout), latency budget, behaviour on empty/malformed input, retraining frequency.

q: Why can't ML functions be fully specified, and what replaces the specification?
short: The mapping (e.g. pixels → objects) has no compact rule humans can write; it is defined implicitly by data. The spec becomes data requirements, labelled evaluation sets, metrics with thresholds, slice-level requirements and operational constraints.
follow: How do you handle edge cases?

q: Design the team and process for taking a fraud model from prototype to production.
short: Data engineers (streaming features), data scientists (model, evaluation), ML engineers (serving, monitoring, retraining), SRE/DevOps (infra), QA (data/model/system tests), product owner (goals/thresholds), security/compliance; agile with ML stages and shared definitions of done.

q: How does continuous delivery for ML differ from classic CD?
short: Pipelines are triggered by code, data and model changes; artifacts include datasets and models; tests include data validation and model evaluation; promotion depends on metrics, and production monitoring feeds retraining.

q: What are the engineering trade-offs of using a third-party foundation model API?
short: Pros: no training, strong capability, fast start. Cons: cost per token, latency, rate limits, vendor lock-in, data privacy, version changes outside your control, limited explainability; mitigate with evaluation suites, abstraction layers, caching, fallbacks.
mistakes: No regression tests when the vendor updates.

q: Where do most failures occur in ML systems and why?
short: In the lower levels and the glue: data collection, pipelines, feature consistency, serving infrastructure and monitoring, because they are larger, less glamorous and less tested than the model code.

q: A model's accuracy is fine offline but complaints rise in production. Walk through the investigation.
short: Check data drift and schema changes, training-serving skew, slice performance, latency/timeouts, recent code/data/model versions (reproduce), label delays; compare live predictions with ground truth; roll back if needed.
detail: Requires versioning and monitoring from day one.
example: Churn v1 after a competitor launch.
follow: What would you monitor next time?
